claims.text: From January 2019 through June 2023, UBS FSI’s supervision failures resulted in thousands of foreign currency wire transfers through retail customer commodity accounts being either insufficiently monitored or omitted from AML transaction monitoring due to deficiencies in system configuration and data governance practices. The firm used a manually generated report that failed to capture all relevant FX wires and was not designed to detect suspicious activity patterns, despite being aware of these vulnerabilities from prior enforcement actions by other agencies. UBS FSI later adopted an automated system in 2021 but failed to properly configure data inputs, which compromised the system’s ability to monitor suspicious activity effectively.

evidence.quote: The order finds from January 2019 through June 2023, due to deficiencies in UBS FSI’s configuration of the relevant surveillance tools and data governance practices, thousands of FX wires sent or received through retail customer commodity accounts the firm held were either insufficiently monitored or omitted from transaction monitoring for AML compliance.

For part of the relevant period, UBS FSI used a manually generated report that failed to capture all relevant FX wires for monitoring and was not tailored to identify patterns of suspicious activity in FX wire transactions.
UBS FSI was aware of these vulnerabilities because they were the subject of prior enforcement proceedings by other government agencies and a self-regulatory organization.
In 2021, UBS FSI transitioned to using an automated system to monitor all wire transactions for suspicious activity.
UBS FSI, however, failed to properly configure the data flowing into the new system, causing issues that impacted the efficacy of its suspicious activity monitoring function.

implications.text: The CFTC’s enforcement action underscores the importance of rigorous oversight over the configuration and data flow into AML transaction monitoring systems, particularly for high-risk activities like FX wire transfers. This highlights the risk of operational oversight lapses persisting despite technological improvements.

executive_summary.text: The CFTC ordered UBS Financial Services Inc. to pay an $8 million penalty for failing to diligently supervise its anti-money laundering (AML) transaction monitoring systems for foreign currency (FX) wire transfers from January 2019 to June 2023. The firm’s inadequate configuration of surveillance tools and data governance led to thousands of FX wires being insufficiently monitored or omitted from AML monitoring, despite prior enforcement notices about similar vulnerabilities. UBS FSI transitioned to an automated monitoring system in 2021 but failed to properly configure data inputs, undermining the system’s effectiveness.

evidence.quote: WASHINGTON — The Commodity Futures Trading Commission today announced an order filing and settling charges against UBS Financial Services Inc., a registered futures commission merchant, for failing to diligently supervise the configuration and operation of its anti-money laundering transaction monitoring systems for wire transfers denominated in foreign currencies (FX).
Under the order, UBS FSI must pay an $8 million civil monetary penalty and cease and desist from further violations of the Commodity Exchange Act and CFTC regulations.

The order finds from January 2019 through June 2023, due to deficiencies in UBS FSI’s configuration of the relevant surveillance tools and data governance practices, thousands of FX wires sent or received through retail customer commodity accounts the firm held were either insufficiently monitored or omitted from transaction monitoring for AML compliance.

For part of the relevant period, UBS FSI used a manually generated report that failed to capture all relevant FX wires for monitoring and was not tailored to identify patterns of suspicious activity in FX wire transactions.
In 2021, UBS FSI transitioned to using an automated system to monitor all wire transactions for suspicious activity.
UBS FSI, however, failed to properly configure the data flowing into the new system, causing issues that impacted the efficacy of its suspicious activity monitoring function.
